newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom chief sparks cultural revolution.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom chief sparks cultural revolution.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom customers angered over phone installation delays, service disruptions or high phone bills are discovering an unknown side of the German phone giant: service with a smile.

Bringing to an end the era of bureacratic indifference to customers is nothing short of a cultural revolution that can be credited to Ron Sommer, Telekom's 47-year-old chief executive, who hones friendliness as a strategic weapon.

"We want to become the most customer-friendly company on the global telecommunications market so that our customers enjoy working with us and forget about the competition," he said at the time of his appointment in May 1995.

Behind Sommer's efforts to modernise Deutsche Telekom is his desire to see the company viewed by the public not as a bloated and indifferent state monolith, but rather as the flagship of German technology laying the groundwork for the international competitiveness of Germany's industry.
While most of the pieces for Telekom's privatisation were in place at the time of his appointment, Sommer was expected to complete the company's transformation.
His background prepared him well for the task.
Born in 1949 in Haifa, Israel, the son of a Russian father and Hungarian mother, he grew up in Vienna, Austria, where in 1971 he earned his doctorate in mathematics at the age of 21.
He went to the United States in 1973 to work for a small computer firm that was later bought by Germany's Nixdorf Computer AG, itself now a division of Siemens AG.
From then on, his career moved fast.
In 1977 he took charge of Nixdorf's operations in France and two years later of its entire international business.
He joined the German subsidiary of consumer electronics giant Sony Corp in 1980, was appointed to the board two years later and in 1986 became Sony's top man in Germany.

After leading Sony to the position of undisputed leader on the German market, he was appointed deputy president of Sony Corp of America in 1990 and its president and chief executive officer in 1991. He became president of Sony Europe in 1993.

The liberalisation of the European telecommunications market in 1998 was clearly visible on the horizon and posed both an opportunity and threat to monopoly Deutsche Telekom when Sommer was appointed chairman last year.
A sharp contrast to the bureacrats at Telekom, the dapper-dressed Sommer appeared to give the company's global aspirations the final stamp of credibility as he quickly pursued three main objectives.

He was determined to make customer service a doctrine of faith, drive international expansion to offset loss of market share to competitors at home, and wage a two-front battle against domestic challengers and regulators to keep market share losses to a minimum.
Telekom has, in fact, become friendlier and more responsive to its customers.
With a management board now dominated by outsiders with years of industry experience, Telekom has become more flexible in its decision-making.
Sommer has also deftly handled one of the most sensitive issues facing the company -- the need to boost productivity by cutting staff as it modernises its vast communications network.
In 1994, the company announced it would cut staff to 170,000 by the year 2000, a reduction of 60 percent. But most analysts believe that is only the starting point.
Sommer faces resistance from the Postal Worker's Union, which has seen its membership dwindle as Telekom cuts jobs.
Calling this his hardest task, Sommer has remained unconfrontational. "We are seeking dialogue," he said.
-- Bonn Newsroom, 49 228 26097145
